 Babbling Brooks: Daylight Saving Time 
 By Carol Brooks 
 Nov 4, 2026

 Well. It happened again. Daylight Saving Time ended early this past Sunday morning, despite U.S. Senate discussion to make it year round and with backing by President Trump. The U.S. House passed the bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, in July by 308-117 vote. 
 So, we were again forced to change clocks, a practice begun in the 1960s. Yes, in the fall we get an extra hour of sleep but that means it will be darker earlier in the day — right when many people are getting off work at 5 p.m. 
 However, children would have an extra hour of daylight to get to school. 
 Reuters News Media quoted Trump in an Oct. 3 column: “Trump said in a social media post that changing the clocks twice a year ‘costs our country a fortune, is bad for crime, stress on people, sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.’” 
 An Associated Press poll in 2025 found only 12 percent of Americans were in favor of Daylight Saving Time. 
 The country tried a trial period of permanent Daylight Saving Time From January 1974-April 1975 but it did not last. By October, the public had demanded the country go back to standard time in the fall. 
 I actually like daylight saving time, preferring the extra hour of daylight during the fall and winter. It is already lighter in the summer, even until 9 p.m. at times, so most people have finished outdoor work or exercise long before it gets dark. 
 Some senators believe the matter will not be discussed again while others are optimistic. 
 “It’s dead as disco,” Republican Sen. John Kennedy told Reuters of the push to make Daylight Saving Time permanent. “My sense is it would have trouble passing … I don’t think the leader is going to bring it up.” 
 Republican Sen. Rick Scott, a key sponsor, told Reuters he was still confident it could be approved when lawmakers return. 
 USA Today recently reported how the fall time change affects us. 
 “Turning clocks back by one hour means sunset arrives earlier and evenings grow darker sooner. That shift can disrupt the body’s circadian rhythm, the internal clock that regulates sleep and other biological functions, potentially affecting health and overall well-being. 
 “The time change also has been linked to fatigue, depression and metabolic changes that may contribute to weight gain, according to Tufts University School of Medicine. 
 “The time change can be especially challenging for teenagers, night-shift workers and older adults, all of whom are more likely to have sleep schedules that are already disrupted, according to [Dr. David] Kuhlmann.” 
 Kuhlmann is a medical director of sleep medicine and spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation. 
 So, now that clocks are turned back, we get an extra hour of sleep — unless you have a hungry cat.
